title: Sorry, I mean thank you

hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Are you a polite person? Guess: what does Sam say when someone steps on his foot?

chapters.title: Sorry, sorry, sorry

chapters.title: Tea first

chapters.title: No pause

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is manners. And I have to say sorry first.
Sorry for what?
Nothing! That's the problem. British people say sorry all the time. Someone steps on my foot, and I say sorry.
[laugh] That's too polite, Sam.
I know. What surprised me in Baku was the respect for older people.
Yes. On the bus, young people always stand up for an older person. Not doing it is really rude.
And at Mr Aliyev's house, I learned you never say no to tea.
Never! Tea is the first thing a guest gets. Saying no is almost an insult.
Then there is small talk. Here a taxi driver asked me how much I earn — in the first minute!
[chuckle] What did you say?
In England we say: bite your tongue. So I just smiled and talked about the weather.
In my family, people interrupt each other all the time. It's not rude — it means we're interested.
At my first dinner with your family, I waited for a pause. There was no pause! [laugh]
My grandmother is strict about one thing: the table. When Aysu takes food before the guests, she says, "Mind your manners!"
My mum said exactly the same to me. In English!
So what's the most important rule for you?
A real apology. Not my automatic "sorry" — a real one, when you are wrong.
I agree. And showing respect to everyone, from the cleaner to the boss.
Well said. Sorry, I mean — thank you. [chuckle]
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is polite in your country but rude somewhere else?
Tell us — and don't interrupt your partner! See you next time!
Bye for now!
